syllabus.quote: Writing an algorithm using pseudocode to solve a given problem, including: – INPUT/READ – WRITE/PRINT – FOR…NEXT – FOR…NEXT…STEP – IF...ELSE...ENDIF – WHILE...ENDWHILE – REPEAT...UNTIL – CASE...ENDCASE

syllabus.quote: Writing and editing a given algorithm that demonstrates a decision-making process, including: – conditional branching – looping – nested loops – procedures/subroutines

words.note: Not in the command-word table (page 66). Topic 4.1 wording.

one_line: Use the syllabus pseudocode keywords or flowchart symbols. Set your variables to a starting value before the loop. Put the counter update inside the loop. Close every structure (ENDIF, ENDWHILE, UNTIL). Label every decision Yes and No.

points.text: Examiners give one mark for each required feature, such as initialising a variable, the loop, the input, the counter update and the output. Most features get a mark on their own, so you can earn marks even if part of your answer is wrong. A few marks depend on other marks. Always attempt the question. The examiner reports say the easier marks are generally there to get.

cites.quote: Eight from: Input number of numbers Initialise count Initialise total Loop that works involving REPEAT… UNTIL (e.g. count = n) Input number within loop Increment count within loop Update total within loop
Initialise Count before Mark variable is input (1) • REPEAT in correct logical location (1) • Input Mark (1)

While questions about flowcharts and pseudocode often test a range of skills, easier marks are generally accessible, making it disappointing to see some candidates choose not to attempt this question.

points.text: Initialise counters and totals before the loop starts, not inside it. In June 2025 Paper 13 Q7, this was the most common mistake among otherwise strong candidates. In Q13 of the same paper, a missing initialisation was the usual reason for losing marks.

cites.quote: most candidates realised that the algorithm required a count and that this count should be initialised outside of the loop. However, a sizeable minority placed the initialisation of the count within the loop.
Where candidates did not achieve full marks, this was generally because they did not initialise the variable Sum.
Two variables (e.g. MAX, COUNT, TOTAL, NUM) initialised/set to zero before loop (1)

points.text: Put the counter increment inside the loop. If the increment is only inside an IF within the loop, it does not get the mark. Make the loop stop at the right value.

cites.quote: Correct Increment of Count (1) • Increment of Count is within the loop (1) • UNTIL Count = 20 (1) • UNTIL in correct position (1)
count ← count + 1 (if within while statement but not if within IF statement (unless in both)

points.text: Use the structures and keywords from the syllabus (IF...ELSE...ENDIF, WHILE...ENDWHILE, REPEAT...UNTIL, CASE...ENDCASE). If the question names a structure, use it. Students who mixed CASE with IF statements lost marks. Students who wrote prose also lost marks. Cambridge publishes a pseudocode guide that shows the expected layout.

cites.quote: Performance on the algorithm question was improved, although some candidates did not use the coding structures and terms given for this qualification.
Most candidates tried to combine the structure with IF statements, thereby highlighting this lack of understanding.
proved challenging to candidates who wrote their answer in prose rather than using algorithmic constructs.
Centres are reminded that CIE has produced a pseudocode guide for teachers and candidates working on this course.

points.text: Small syntax errors cost marks. Write each comparison in full (IF X > Y AND X < Z, not IF X > Y and < Z). Close every IF with ENDIF. Input or output each variable separately ('OUTPUT smallest and largest' was not accepted). Put text in speech marks, with commas between text and variables.

cites.quote: treating the test criteria as a string and using the structure IF X>Y and <Z, instead of IF X>Y AND X<Z.
Failure to close IF statements with ENDIF statements. • Failure to use mathematical reasoning in the pseudocode.
For example, some responses stated, “Output smallest and largest”, which would not work and so was not accepted.

Using an input statement ‘input X and Y’. This would not correctly input the values for the two variables. • Not indenting within the IF statement and not closing the IF statement. • Not using speech marks and commas within the outputs

points.text: Indent the lines inside IF, ELSE and loops. Some mark schemes give a mark just for correct indentation. Variable names with two or more words must have no spaces. Examiners do not take off marks for a slightly wrong variable name if it is clear which variable you mean.

cites.quote: IF and ENDIF indented correctly (1) • Use of THEN (1)
Where marks were awarded, these tended to be for structural awareness, such as correct use of indentation, or for inputting a number at the start of the process.
It should be noted that where variable names are made up of two or more words, there should be no gap between these words.
(Ignore errors with variable names, as long as it is clear which variable is being referred to)

points.text: In a flowchart, every decision box needs two exits labelled Yes and No (True and False are accepted). Write the condition as a maths expression, not in words. For example, 'is x between 5 and 10' is not acceptable.

cites.quote: Candidates are reminded that all decision boxes must have a Yes and a No output (True and False are acceptable) and that they should use mathematical expression rather than text in their boxes. For example, the term ‘is x between 5 and 10’ is not acceptable.
Firstly, decisions need to be based on questions, and each decision has two outcomes. These outcomes may be yes/no, or true/false, but they must be shown and labelled.

points.text: Use the symbols shown in the syllabus: parallelograms for input and output, rectangles for processes, and terminators for Start and Stop. Do not mix up input and process boxes, and do not use other versions of the symbols. Mark schemes give marks for correct shapes and for arrowheads on flow lines.

cites.quote: Candidates need to use the symbols provided by the board and should have practiced using them correctly.
In a small number of cases, candidates confused input symbols with process symbols

While it is accepted that there are variations on the use of symbols and their naming in system flowcharts, it is expected that for the purposes of this syllabus that the symbols shown in the syllabus be used.
All lines have arrow heads with direction of flow 1 mark 9 All correct symbols/shapes 1 mark

points.text: Do exactly what the question asks. If it says 'redraw', draw a new flowchart rather than editing the printed one. If it asks for a flowchart, do not write pseudocode. Include every feature the question lists, such as a calculation and an output.

cites.quote: In this question, candidates were clearly asked to redraw the flowchart. Candidates who amended the original flowchart and did not provide a new flowchart were therefore not answering the question.
In a very small number of cases, candidates gave a form of pseudocode, instead of a flowchart for the answer
As a general comment on questions such as these, most candidates did not include all features identified in the question.

points.text: When you suggest or describe a change to a flowchart or pseudocode, say exactly where it goes. For example, say which line you remove and what replaces it. Write the answer in the answer space, not on the printed code.

cites.quote: candidates need to be extremely clear about which line is being removed, and how it is to be replaced.
centres are advised that candidates should answer the question in the space provided in the question paper, rather than writing answers on the pseudocode included in the question paper.

question.quote: Write a pseudocode algorithm using REPEAT...UNTIL which allows the teacher to input 20 test marks and outputs the correct message for each inputted mark.

examples.context: Marks above 70 get a Distinction. Marks from 55 to 70 get a Merit, and marks from 40 to 54 get a Pass. Marks below 40 get the message 'You have not reached the Pass mark'.

earns.quote: Initialise Count before Mark variable is input (1)

strong.sentence: IF Mark > 70 THEN PRINT "You have achieved a Distinction" ENDIF   and   IF Mark < 40 THEN PRINT "You have not reached the Pass mark" ENDIF

earns.quote: Correct Distinction grade criterion//correct fail criterion (1)

strong.sentence: IF Mark > 54 AND Mark < 71 THEN PRINT "You have achieved a Merit" ENDIF

earns.quote: Correct Merit grade criterion//correct Pass grade criterion (1)

strong.sentence: IF Mark > 39 AND Mark < 55 THEN PRINT "You have achieved a Pass" ENDIF

earns.quote: Correct Increment of Count (1) • Increment of Count is within the loop (1)

strong.sentence: UNTIL Count = 20   (as the last line of the loop)

earns.quote: UNTIL Count = 20 (1) • UNTIL in correct position (1)

strong.sentence: Every PRINT message matches its range of marks.

earns.quote: All OUTPUTs correctly match the criteria (NOT awardable if BP4 or BP5 not awarded) (1)

weak.answer:
REPEAT
    Count ← 0
    INPUT Mark
    IF Mark >= 55 and <= 70 THEN OUTPUT "You have achieved a Merit"
    ...
    Count ← Count + 1
UNTIL Count = 20
weak.why: The code sets Count to 0 on every pass, so the loop never ends and the answer loses the initialisation mark. The Merit test does not repeat the variable (it should be Mark > 54 AND Mark < 71), and the IF has no ENDIF. The answer can still get the REPEAT, INPUT, increment and UNTIL marks.

basis.quote: However, a sizeable minority placed the initialisation of the count within the loop. This was the most frequently made mistakes amongst candidates who otherwise had a strong understanding of what was required.

examples.note: This is pseudocode, so the strong answer is lines of code, not sentences. The lines cover more than eight mark-scheme points, and the mark is capped at 8. The increment and UNTIL lines earn two points each. The syllabus lists only the comparison operators >, < and =, and it lists WRITE/PRINT for output. So the ranges use > and < (marks are whole numbers), and the output uses PRINT. The mark scheme's own example uses OUTPUT. Most of the marks are for structure. Initialise before the loop, increment inside it, and use the right UNTIL condition in the right place.

question.quote: Draw a program flowchart to represent this algorithm: • Input an integer value. • Repeat this until you have entered 20 values. • At the end, output the largest value and the average of the values.

strong.sentence: Start with a Start terminator and finish with an End (or Stop) terminator.
In a process rectangle before the loop, set COUNT and TOTAL to 0.

earns.quote: Two variables (e.g. MAX, COUNT, TOTAL, NUM) initialised/set to zero before loop (1)

strong.sentence: Use parallelograms for every input of NUM and for the output of MAX and the average.

earns.quote: Input box and output box are both parallelograms (1)

strong.sentence: Input the first NUM and set MAX ← NUM. Then, inside the loop, use process rectangles for TOTAL ← TOTAL + NUM and COUNT ← COUNT + 1.

earns.quote: Sum all values input (1) 11 Set new MAX when input value > MAX in loop 12 Increment COUNT (1)

strong.sentence: Draw two decision diamonds, 'NUM > MAX?' and 'COUNT = 20?', each with labelled Yes and No exits.

earns.quote: TWO Correctly drawn decision boxes with YES/NO decisions (1)

strong.sentence: From 'NUM > MAX?', Yes goes to MAX ← NUM and No skips it. From 'COUNT = 20?', No goes to an input box for the next NUM and back into the loop, and Yes leaves the loop.

earns.quote: All YES/NO decisions (used) go to correct outcomes (i.e. all logic is correct) (1)

strong.sentence: After the loop, calculate AVERAGE ← TOTAL / 20 in a process rectangle.

weak.answer: A flowchart that puts 'Input number' in a rectangle, has a decision box 'Have 20 numbers been entered' with no Yes or No labels, and never sets COUNT or TOTAL to zero.
weak.why: It uses the wrong symbol for input, writes the decision in words without Yes/No labels, and leaves out the initialisation before the loop.

basis.quote: In a small number of cases, candidates confused input symbols with process symbols, but overall, performance on this question was very good.

examples.note: The mark scheme lists 14 features that earn marks, for 7 marks. So if you get the shapes, labels and initialisation right, you have room to spare. MAX starts at the first value, not 0, so the answer still works if every number is negative. The mark scheme also accepts setting MAX to 0. The weak answer describes a flowchart in words, because this guide cannot show a drawing.

thin_evidence: Evidence is strong for pseudocode and program flowcharts in Paper 1. Many questions from 2022 onward have examiner comments. The June 2022 examiner report says several times that algorithms and flowcharts were a recent addition to the syllabus. So the most recent reports (2024-2025) are the best guide. Draw also covers DFD, PERT and system-flowchart questions in Paper 3. Only the symbol points here apply to those. 'Write' is sometimes tagged on parts that are not about algorithms. Examples are November 2025 Paper 11 and Paper 13 Q8(b), which are about audio. This guide ignores those parts.
